newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak govt may ask for return of bank selloff law.
newsitem.headline: Slovak govt may ask for return of bank selloff law.

text.p: The Slovak government is considering asking President Michal Kovac not to sign a law barring bank privatisation and return it to parliament, the government spokeswoman said on Tuesday.

"The government asked Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik and Deputy Prime Minister Katarina Tothova to work out material to argue the return of the law to parliament," Magda Pospisilova told journalists after a regular government meeting.
Pospisilova said the government should discuss the document and decide on its fate next Tuesday. She declined to elaborate further.
Last Thursday, parliament approved a measure effectively halting bank privatisation until the end of the year 2003 at the earliest.
The law bars privatisation of shares owned by the state or the National Property Fund (the state privatisation agency).

According to the Slovak constitution, the president must return a law to the parliament at the request of the government. A law becomes effective when it is signed by both the prime minister and president.

Through the NPF, the state controls 91.3 percent of the largest savings bank Slovenska Sporitelna, 50.5 percent in the major insurance company Slovenska Poistovna, some 35 percent in bank IRB and about 17 percent in the largest commercial bank VUB.
The Czech National Property Fund also holds about 33 percent in VUB.

Last June, bank privatisation was at the heart of a crisis within Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's ruling coalition consisting of his Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), the ultra-right Slovak National Party and the ultra-left Workers' Party (ZRS) which was against the selloff.
The rift was eventually settled and parliament then approved a measure postponing the bank privatisation until March 31, 1997.

Political and economic analysts say the current row over banking privatisation inside the coalition may indicate another serious crisis between the coalition parties since one of its members voted together with the opposition on the law.
Opposition parties and ZRS said they would again vote for the postponement of bank privatisation if the government uses its right asking the president to return the law to parliament.
The government has said it was necessary to privatise the banks as soon as possible to fulfil conditions for membership into international economic organisations, such as the OECD.
The OECD, however, warned Slovakia last year against too quick a bank selloff, saying the restructuring of state- controlled financial institutions was more crucial.
